utterances.text: What file at what police station?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Srebrenica police station where I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dangerous to speculate and I'm not inviting you to speculate and if you can only answer this question by speculation, then don't, okay? But can you think of anyone who would have any good -- any reason to complete this form other than yourself? If you can't that's fair enough; I don't want you to speculate. But if you know of anyone who would have a reason, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Move on to the other part of the document and that is the part which appears to have been signed by Mr. -- a Mr. Oric. Would you have a look at that document? It's headed, "Opinion and proposal of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica." Just quickly cast your eye over that document.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this document. In fact, I read it here and I think that it contains quite a lot of illogical and inaccurate things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make a few comments, this document first of all does not have a date when it was written. That's number 1. Number 2, here it says that on the 14th of December 1992, I was wounded at Kunjarac, which is not correct. I was wounded on the 16th of December 1992. It says here that I was a deputy police commander, and I have already said that at that time, I was at the front line and I was the leader of the Kazani group. I was never deputy or I was never involved in the military police at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it from your evidence that you regard this document with mistrust, you don't think its authentic and you've never seen it before, not until you came to The Hague, any way, correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric ever intercede on your behalf or do anything on your behalf in respect of your joining any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, except on that one occasion when he wanted to dismiss me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that -- your evidence about that. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, can I tender those documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to tender them as one document or separate, two documents. MR. DI FAZIO: I think as one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, too, but, Madam Registrar, what's the next number, approximate Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 611. So this will become Prosecution Exhibit P611. Before we set it aside, if someone could help me. At the -- on the first page of this document, right at the very top right-hand corner, above the ERN number, there is something handwritten there which is not reflected in the English translation. I would like to know if that makes sense to anyone who can read B/C/S. Can anyone indicate to us what those letters and digits mean or -- MR. DI FAZIO: I can. It seems to be a combination of letters and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is what I'm asking. I don't see a reflection of it in the English translation. MR. DI FAZIO: No it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But -- MR. DI FAZIO: I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask the witness, of course. I asked for assistance basically if someone can help me there but, to me, it doesn't mean anything when I look at it but equally I don't see a reason why it's not reflected in the English translation. At least as far as the letters and the numbers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes apparently -- in Bosnian, it doesn't mean anything apparently. Apparently it indicates a collection, the name of the collection this is from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This type of designation is put on some collections. The words itself, the designation itself does not have any meaning in the Bosnian language but we have noticed such marks made on some other documents we received from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it mean anything to you, Mr. Smajlovic? At the top right-hand corner, you see those -- there are eight numbers. On top of that, there are some letters handwritten and some numbers. It looks like CA -- I don't know because I don't even know if that is a Latin --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We can leave it at that, then. Are you finished with your cross-examination, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: On this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to return briefly to the meeting at Bajramovici again. Just two small topics. At the meeting, was Akif Ustic appointed the deputy coordinator, the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his role supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who -- did anyone propose him, that he be appointed deputy coordinator of local groups?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same people that I spoke before. Some -- somebody said Akif and then that was supported. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was -- how did the support manifest itself? Was it a show of hands or was a vote taken? Did the crowd vocally indicate the support of these appointments? How did it actually happen?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the people vocally indicated that this person or that person should be appointed and that the body itself could make decisions only by vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in the months that ensued, June, July, August, September, October, November, December and January, February, and March of 1993, how many occasions were votes taken on any actions that Mr. Oric took as coordinator? I'm talking about 1993 -- 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend those meetings because I was on the front line, in the areas where the attacks were occurring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of votes being taken? I'm referring now to your evidence yesterday that it was -- that Mr. Oric couldn't actually do anything, couldn't take any decisions, and everything had to be put to the vote. What I'm asking is how many votes -- how many occasions did voting occur in those months in 1992 and 1993 on issues that were --

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said a little while ago, I was not there. I don't know. I was at the front line where the fiercest attacks were occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has testified that he was present when the decision was taken to make decisions in the future but vote. He did not say that he had actually been present when those further events took place. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine. And I think the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. And he's confirmed it. MR. DI FAZIO: He's confirmed it again, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of any votes being taken, even though you weren't present?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear of any because I did not have the time to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Oric quite often, didn't you, in -- throughout 1992 and early parts of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But we never discussed those things. We only discussed the issue how to stop the Chetniks' advance on those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that -- I can't recall when precisely but you said in evidence that he came to your group at one stage, the Kazani group, and had some dispute with you. I think that was the effect of your evidence, that he wanted to remove you as leader and that you -- anyway, the result was that you remained as leader. Do you remember that -- that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any vote taken on that particular issue, your removal as leader of the Kazani group? Was that put to the vote, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. I know that he came and I know what happened, and that's what I actually already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, bearing in mind his role as coordinator amongst local leaders, did you consider saying to Mr. Oric, "Mr. Oric, this is a matter that needs a vote."? Did you consider that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It never occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were also asked some questions about Exhibit P4. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me? I may not have to produce it. No. I think it's probably better I do. Can the witness be shown P4?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember this document, it was shown to you yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic asked you -- sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me withdraw that question. This is a document, obviously you can see on the face of it it's apparently comes from this body called the Srebrenica TO. And under number 10, item number 10, C, there appears a phrase, "At the VP, the organisation to be carried out by Mirzet Halilovic." Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that it's written there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, VP, is that military police, Vojna policija or something like that? Pardon my B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remember giving evidence that this document, P4, that's not correct, because, in fact, the military police were set up by the War Presidency. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that the War Presidency had established the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And, look, apart from that fact, that you say is wrong at number 10(C), is there anything else on the face of the document that you can see that makes you suspicious of it or causes you any concern about its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: TO Osmace, Mirsad Dudic was the group leader there and the organiser. Atif Krdzic was not there in that capacity ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And likewise, whether it comes to TO Kragljivoda, Nedzad Bektic was never the group leader there. It was Sefik Mandzic. Furthermore, Luka TO, Ikan Mujic was the group leader. It was not definitely not Mustafa Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough to say this: What causes you concern about there document is the content but there is nothing on the actual -- in the actual writing or on the face of the document, on the page, that causes you any concern other than that? It's the inaccuracies of the information, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are quite a few inaccuracies when it comes to the services, where it says war hospital, Avdo Hasanovic. I explained yesterday that the war hospital was actually located in my home and, furthermore, the signals and information service, Hamed Alic was appointed, and on the 20th of May 1992, Hamed Alic was a survivor of an execution, both his wife and his father were killed on that occasion, and at that time he was very much distressed, in a shock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you -- this passage of evidence occurred in relation to this document, and the military police.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was mentioned for the first time on the 1st of July 1992. You could see from other documents that Mirzet Halilovic was group leader of the Pale group up until the 1st of July. This document is dated 15 June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, really my question is this, I suppose: If there is no military operating in the area of Srebrenica in 1992, and the first three months of 1993, there is no army, no military, just local leaders leading groups, what -- why is it necessary to have a military police? Why did the War Presidency find it necessary? Why?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency had the following considerations. There were people, armed, who were out of anyone's control, walking around the town, and both the civilian and the military police had the duty to keep these people under control, to disarm them, and both the civilian and the military police forces were under the command of Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well. I understand what you're saying about the War Presidency and its role in setting up a military police, and I understand what you say about the dangerous and uncertain times and with people walking around being armed. But why set up specifically a military police? Why not simply have a police force to deal with these armed people? Why is it necessary to have a civilian police and a military police if there is no military? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the description of his post, it was never within the duties of a military police officer to disarm people. It was always within the competence of the civilian police. And we didn't know what to do but therefore decided to put it under the command of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. With respect, Mr. Smajlovic, I suggest that you're not answering my question. I'll be as clear as I can. Okay? The War Presidency set up a military police - you've told us this - and they did it on July, I think, and this is wrong, this document, P4. Now, and you've testified this morning and yesterday and the day before that there was no army, no military, operating in Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993. Okay? So why have a military police if there is no military? If there is a simple explanation, tell us and I'll move on, but I want to know that.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there is no simple explanation for that. I told you that the civilian police officers cannot disarm armed men. They are there to maintain law and order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there had been an existing army structure in -- operating in Srebrenica in 1992, and early parts of 1993, you would have expected that structure to create or appoint or deal with or control a military police, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain this to you in view of my military experience. The military police was never under any staffs of the Territorial Defence. It always came under corps or brigades. Since there was no TO staff set up and there were no brigades or corps in Srebrenica, it could not come under a military structure. We didn't know what else to do but to place it under the command of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the civilian police differ from the military police? Did they -- I assume they didn't have uniforms because no one had uniforms, correct? But in what other way -- what ways did they differ from each other?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They differed from each other in that the civilian police had an additional task which was to restore law and order among the population. It was in charge of disorderly conduct. Whereas the military police will no business there. It could only, together with the civilian police, disarm people who carried weapons in Srebrenica and were out of anyone's control. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember the military police ever arresting anyone or dealing with them for military -- some sort of military infringement? Some sort of military offence, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only thing the military police did was seize weapons. For everything else the civilian police was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Seize weapons from whom precisely? Civilians walking around or fighters in the local groups? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They seized weapons from civilians who -- as they entered Srebrenica, whenever they went in search of something they would find wherever, be it in a ditch or on a meadow or amidst garbage they would find pieces of weapons that had been abandoned by the Serbs who had been retreating from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why couldn't the civilian -- I don't understand that, with respect, Mr. Smajlovic. Why couldn't the civilian police go and get these unfortunate people who were carrying arms, these civilians, why couldn't they perform that task? Why was it necessary for the military police to do that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were unable to. At the time there were about 30.000 refugees in Srebrenica. What can a handful of police officers do in the face of such a large crowd of people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see how this particular witness would be able to answer such a line of hypothetical questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you that we are in hypothetical areas here because he was by profession a policeman. He formed part of the civilian police at a certain time. So when Mr. Di Fazio asks him to explain why a civilian police wouldn't have been able to do that, I mean he's perfectly capable of giving an answer. So let's proceed along these lines. I don't know if you are satisfied with his answer already, Mr. Di Fazio, or not, whether you want to proceed with this matter or pursue it any further. MR. DI FAZIO: I think we'll leave it, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already told you more than once that they were unable to do so. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, one last question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the weapons that were seized from the -- that the military police seized from the civilians?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. I was not privy to that. Probably they were handed over to the groups that found themselves in the most vulnerable areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you do that. Judge Eser, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to wrap up this question with military and civilian police, did I understand you correctly that you said the civil -- military police was necessary because the civil police was not big enough, didn't have enough people, to get hold of the problem of disarming people? Was this your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was not my answer. The civilian police has a totally different set of duties that it's in charge of. That was the case yesterday. That was the case at the time, and is today. It never had within its duties the duty to disarm people and collect the weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But I think that in quite a few countries to be in possession of illegal arms would be an offence and then the civil police would have jurisdiction to deal with this problem. Is that different -- or has that been different in your country, that disarming people would be a matter of military police and not of civil police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That may be the case in peacetime, but not in time of war, when you don't know what belongs where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I show the documents I just want to ask you some other questions. You were wounded in 1992 in Kunjarac, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you wounded again in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And your father's name is Avdo. What year was he born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he -- did he fight at all during the war?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? Where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that he was wounded in his leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we misunderstood each other, where, geographically, where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know when or where he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was he in your group?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, would this be an appropriate moment to ask the witness to call it quits for the day? I still have that submission to go and I also seek a little -- I mean I can finish my submission probably before one but I would just like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to finish it by one, because by one, one of us has to leave. Mr. Smajlovic we have to stop here for the day. We will continue on Monday. Please try and rest as much as you can. It has been a long week for you here, and I want to make sure that you receive all the attention you require to be able to rest throughout the weekend. We will continue and finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you deal with that, how much longer do you require this witness, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't want to disrupt the schedule anticipated for next week. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I'm going to be -- take a goodly portion of Monday. I don't know what -- how that affects the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How does that affect not only the Defence but also us because we have the responsibility of managing the trial. There are two witnesses and the time-frame indicated to us inclusive of Defence and Prosecution -- MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, now that I've got the weekend to go over what I've prepared and what remains to be done for my purposes I can certainly try and streamline matters as much as I can. And I'll do so. I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have got this problem. One is coming from the United States. The other one, I don't know where he is coming from, but he is then going to the Far East with an intimation that we had time back that it's very difficult to bring him back at any -- any time soon. And I have all the responsibility to make sure that we finish with the two witnesses by Friday of next week. The day after we will all be gone. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I understand that, Your Honour, and all the difficulties that we have and I understand your concerns, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want you to not only understand but also sit down, discuss it with your lead counsel, and also coordinate with the Defence, in the spirit that we have advocated throughout. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour can -- you will have my utmost cooperation in trying to keep what I have for Monday as brief as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Submission on this fresh Rule 68 allegation. MR. DI FAZIO: It's very, very brief, if Your Honours please. The complaint -- I think the new material, if I understand, is contained in paragraphs 4 to 6, and it is said that the fact of Serb prisoners being taken to the Domavija hotel and then that Mr. Oric would take them to Potocari for exchange is not exculpatory in the sense that it doesn't actually say anything about custody and control and responsibility for the -- for the -- for the prisoners. If it does, the Prosecution's submission is that, in all the circumstances, the prejudice is absolutely minimal, and furthermore, you recall Hakija Meholjic actually testified about Serb prisoners of war being held at the Domavija hotel and he provided that testimony on the 7th of April 2005. I haven't reviewed that testimony because of obvious reasons but I understand that that's the testimony, and you can find it there on the 7th of April 2005, and I recall from his evidence that he did say -- he gave some sort -- I recall that he gave evidence of an occasion when he came to the hotel and he -- there were some Serb prisoners there and they had been mistreated and he leapt to their defence and threw out the men who had mistreated the Serb prisoners. I remember that evidence. So there is some evidence already in the Prosecution case that, indeed, some Serb POWs were taken to the Domavija hotel and from my memory -- would Your Honours just bear with me? That's in examination-in-chief so it was led by the Prosecution. So that's -- those are the submissions that I just wanted to make on that particular paragraph. There has been evidence about it already. We led it. And that's -- so therefore, any prejudice is really got to be minimal. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence would like to address this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just extremely briefly. This is the limb of Rule 68 which concerns the credibility of Prosecution witnesses. Our submission is simply that this is information which goes to the credibility of a Prosecution witness which we should have had in time for the cross-examination of that witness. The fact that it was let's in chief in a way makes the point that in fact if the Prosecution hadn't led that evidence-in-chief, we wouldn't have known about it and we wouldn't have been able to raise it and I just reiterate the submission which is in the reply already, which is that this argument that there is no prejudice isn't really an answer because the point is, unless we have the information in a timely fashion so that we can make our tactical decisions about how to use it, then there is a violation and we ask you to find that there has been one in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. This for your information will be incorporated -- in other words, our decision on this new allegation will be incorporated in the decision that we anticipate to hand down early next week. The idea is to have the drafting completed over the weekend by Monday, then we sit down and discuss it again, the three judges, and then either hand it down on Monday, end of the day, or Tuesday morning. All right? We are going to adjourn now. Please make sure, Mr. Wubben, that the Defence has been given the list of additional topics that Lieutenant Colonel Dudley is authorised to be cross-examined upon by his government, by the US government, as agreed beforehand. I think that you have already given a list which -- have you been given a list which then had to be edited according to the permission granted or withheld by the US government?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, the agreement is that following the interview with Mr. Dudley, that we'll receive a provisional list which the Prosecution is going to submit for authorisation to the USG. So it's that provisional list which I understand we will receive shortly, and then if and when authorisation is received, then I understand we will be informed of that subsequent list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is interviewing? I thought you were going to interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were supposed to start at 2.00, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be starting shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I refer to the agreement? The agreement is indeed as I already stated yesterday that we will provide the Defence after completion of the interview, that should be done now for any moment, we will provide them with a list, an informal list of issues in which there is considered to be no problem on authorisation in that respect because authorisation still has to be -- function as a kind of official decision making but we will provide them with a list as soon as possible. And after this adjournment I will take a contact with Madam Vidovic how to process this information as soon as possible, after this proceeding to her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And we will continue with this witness on Monday. Again, I recommend that you keep in mind the schedule for the next two witnesses, and that definitely, as I read it, would entail four days, four days as a minimum, as a minimum. Definitely more actually, but four days is the absolute minimum that need to be left for those two witnesses. And the indication is that there should also be some additional time to that. So you need to discuss amongst yourselves a little bit how you're going to approach this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good -- have a nice weekend, everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of December 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.56 p.m.,
